Opening Context – Why Server Logs Lie
In the distributed architecture of real-time communications, the server is often the last to know about a degradation in quality. You can scale your Selective Forwarding Units (SFUs) to handle ten thousand concurrent streams, ensure your signaling WebSocket servers have sub-millisecond latency, and provision massive bandwidth headroom, yet your users will still report frozen video and robotic audio. Traditional backend observability relies on server-side logs: socket connection states, ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) completion events, and SFU ingress/egress bitrates. entry.title: Interleaving: Why Mixing Practice Beats Blocking
entry.summary: Traditional advice says practice one thing until you master it, then move to the next. Research says this is backwards. Interleaving—mixing different topics or problem types during practice—produces better learning than blocked practice, even though it feels harder. Blocked practice: AAAA BBBB CCCC (master one type, then the next) Interleaved practice: ABCABCABCA (mix types throughout) Example: Instead of doing 20 multiplication problems, then 20 division, mix them randomly. Discrimination learning: Mixing forces your brain to identify WHICH strategy applies, not just HOW to execute one strategy. Retrieval practice: Each switch requires retrieving the relevant approach from memory, strengthening it. Spacing effect: Interleaving naturally spaces practice of each type. Studies consistently show interleaved practice produces 20-50% better performance on delayed tests, despite worse performance during practice. In one study, students learning to identify painting styles performed 30% better when training was interleaved vs. blocked. Mix problem types in homework and practice sets Study multiple subjects in one session rather than marathoning one Randomize flashcard order rather than grouping by topic Combine old and new material in each practice session After initial learning (you need some competence first) For discriminating between similar concepts For applying knowledge to novel situations Interleaving produces more errors during practice. This is desirable difficulty—the struggle is the learning. Trust the research over your feelings. Long-term retention matters more than practice performance. entry.title: Haar Cascades to YOLO: Face Detection Migration Guide
entry.summary:
The 15-Year-Old Code That Still Runs in Production
Haar Cascades are everywhere. If you've ever used OpenCV's face detector, you've used a method published in 2001. It's older than Python 2.7, slower than YOLO, and somehow still the first thing that appears in every "face detection tutorial" on the internet. But here's the thing: migrating from Haar to YOLO isn't just swapping out a model file. The preprocessing assumptions are different. The output format is completely incompatible. And if you don't handle the transition carefully, you'll silently miss faces or flood your pipeline with false positives. This post walks through a real migration: taking an existing OpenCV face detection pipeline and converting it to YOLOv8. I'll show the code changes, the performance differences, and the three edge cases that broke when I first tried this.

entry.title: How We Taught Our App to Find Medical Lab Results in Gmail
entry.summary: About a year ago, I received a task that seemed simple at first glance: implement a feature to search for PDF files containing medical lab results in Gmail. The idea was straightforward - the user authorizes access to their email through our app, we scan the mailbox for PDFs with lab results and medical data, then display all found documents to the user. After that, the user decides which ones they want to share with us. Sounds simple enough, right? But there's a big catch - Google doesn't just give you access to a user's mailbox. Working with Gmail API requires going through a verification process and getting approval from the Google team. I want to express my gratitude to the Google team for their support and for approving our request. But the hardest part wasn't the approval process itself - it was figuring out how to even approach it. The documentation didn't provide clear answers. An article from another developer who had faced a similar challenge helped me out. It turned out there's one key requirement for getting approved: all operations must be performed strictly on the client side. Since we have a mobile app, all Gmail operations must happen directly on the user's device. Sending tokens, email IDs, or attachment IDs to the backend is strictly prohibited. Everything stays on the client side. The dialogue with the Google team lasted 6 months. And finally, we got the green light. The feature was shipped and warmly received by our users. The moral of the story: sometimes the hardest part of a task isn't the technical solution itself, but figuring out how to get that solution approved by the platform.

entry.title: Mamba-2 vs Griffin vs RWKV-6: SSM Architecture Benchmark
entry.summary:
The Linear-Time Transformer Replacement Everyone's Building
The quadratic complexity of attention — $O(n^2)$ for sequence length $n$ — stopped being theoretical the moment context windows hit 128k tokens. State Space Models (SSMs) promise $O(n)$ complexity without sacrificing quality, but three architectures dominate 2026: Mamba-2, Griffin, and RWKV-6. I benchmarked all three on the same 1.3B parameter budget. The results challenged what I thought I knew about attention alternatives.
Andrey Matveev on Pexels
What Makes SSMs Different From Transformers
Transformers compute attention scores between every token pair. For a 10k token sequence, that's 100M comparisons. SSMs instead maintain a fixed-size hidden state that gets updated sequentially: $$h_t = \bar{A}h_{t-1} + \bar{B}x_t$$ The matrices $\bar{A}, \bar{B}, C$ are learned, but crucially: $h_t$ doesn't grow with sequence length. You process 10 tokens or 100k tokens with the same memory footprint. Continue reading the full article on TildAlice
